questionText: Man facing north turns 135° left, then 225° right. Facing?
hints: This is a turning problem. A left turn and a right turn undo each other, so think about the turn that is left over.
The right turn is bigger than the left turn. Find how many degrees of right turn remain after the left turn is cancelled.
Similar example: a girl faces north, turns 45° left and then 225° right. The turns leave 225° − 45° = 180° to the right. Half a turn from north is south, so she faces south.

stepByStep.text: Turning left and then right cancel each other. The right turn is bigger.
So the man ends up turned 90° to the right from north.
A quarter turn to the right from north points east. He is facing East.

misconceptions.A: This is where he faces after the first turn only. He still has to turn 225° to the right.
misconceptions.B: This would be a turn of 135° to the right from north. The turn left over is 225° − 135° = 90° to the right.
misconceptions.C: Yes! The turns leave 90° to the right, and a quarter turn right from north is east.
misconceptions.D: North-West is on the left side of north. The bigger turn is to the right, so he ends on the right side.

questionText: Angle = 35°. Sum of complementary and supplementary?
hints: This is about complementary and supplementary angles. Complementary angles add up to 90° and supplementary angles add up to 180°.
Find the complement of 35° first by taking it away from 90°. Then find its supplement.
Similar example: for an angle of 20°, the complement is 90° − 20° = 70° and the supplement is 180° − 20° = 160°. Their sum is 70° + 160° = 230°.

stepByStep.text: The complement makes 90° with the angle.
The supplement makes 180° with the angle.
Add the complement and the supplement.
The sum is 200°.

misconceptions.A: Yes! The complement is 55°, the supplement is 145°, and 55° + 145° = 200°.
misconceptions.B: Check both subtractions: 90° − 35° = 55° and 180° − 35° = 145°. Then add them.
misconceptions.C: This is 145° + 35°, the supplement plus the angle itself. Add the complement and the supplement instead.
misconceptions.D: Find both angles first: the complement is 55° and the supplement is 145°. Then add the two.

questionText: Angle = (1/5)th of supplementary. Find angle.
hints: This is a supplementary angle problem with parts. The angle and its supplement together make 180°.
If the angle is 1 part, its supplement is 5 equal parts. Count how many parts make 180° altogether.
Similar example: an angle is one third of its supplement. The angle is 1 part and the supplement is 3 parts, so 4 parts make 180°. One part is 180° ÷ 4 = 45°. The angle is 45°.

stepByStep.text: The angle is one fifth of its supplement. So if the angle is 1 part, the supplement is 5 parts.
Together they make 180°, and that is 6 parts.
Find one part.
Check: the supplement is 150°, and one fifth of 150° is 30°. The angle is 30°.

misconceptions.A: Check it: the supplement of 40° is 140°, and one fifth of 140° is 28°, not 40°.
misconceptions.B: Check it: the supplement of 35° is 145°, and one fifth of 145° is 29°, not 35°.
misconceptions.C: Yes! 30° and 150° make 180°, and 30° is one fifth of 150°.
misconceptions.D: Check it: the supplement of 50° is 130°, and one fifth of 130° is 26°, not 50°.

questionText: Supplementary angle of obtuse angle is always?
hints: This is about types of angles. Think about how big an obtuse angle is and what its supplement must add to it.
An obtuse angle is more than 90° but less than 180°. Its supplement is what is left to reach 180°. Is that more or less than 90°?

Similar example: what kind of angle is the supplement of an acute angle? Try 40°: its supplement is 180° − 40° = 140°. An acute angle is less than 90°, so what is left is always more than 90°. The supplement of an acute angle is always obtuse.

stepByStep.text: An obtuse angle is more than 90° and less than 180°.
Its supplement is 180° take away the angle. Taking away more than 90° leaves less than 90°.
For example, the supplement of 110° is 70°.
An angle less than 90° is acute. So the supplement of an obtuse angle is always an Acute Angle.

misconceptions.A: The supplement would be a right angle only if the angle itself were 90°. An obtuse angle is bigger than 90°.
misconceptions.B: Complementary describes two angles that add up to 90°. Here, ask how big the supplement is.
misconceptions.C: A straight angle is 180° all by itself. The supplement is only the part left over after the obtuse angle.
misconceptions.D: Yes! Taking more than 90° away from 180° always leaves less than 90°, which is an acute angle.

questionText: Sum of complementary and supplementary of 48°?
hints: This is about complementary and supplementary angles. Complementary angles add up to 90° and supplementary angles add up to 180°.
Find the complement of 48° first by taking it away from 90°. Then find its supplement.
Similar example: for an angle of 30°, the complement is 90° − 30° = 60° and the supplement is 180° − 30° = 150°. Their sum is 60° + 150° = 210°.

stepByStep.text: The complement makes 90° with the angle.
The supplement makes 180° with the angle.
Add the complement and the supplement.
The sum is 174°.

misconceptions.A: This is 10° short. The complement is 42° and the supplement is 132°. Add them again.
misconceptions.B: Yes! The complement is 42°, the supplement is 132°, and 42° + 132° = 174°.
misconceptions.C: Check both subtractions: 90° − 48° = 42° and 180° − 48° = 132°. Then add them.
misconceptions.D: This is 10° too much. The complement is 42° and the supplement is 132°. Add them again.

questionText: Sum of complementary and supplementary angles of 48°?
hints: This question has two parts. Find the complementary angle and the supplementary angle of the same angle, then add them.
The complement of 48° is what must be added to 48° to make 90°. Find it first, then find the supplement in the same way with 180°.
Similar example: for an angle of 25°, the complement is 90° − 25° = 65° and the supplement is 180° − 25° = 155°. Their sum is 65° + 155° = 220°.

stepByStep.text: The complement makes 90° with the angle.
The supplement makes 180° with the angle.
Add the complement and the supplement.
The sum is 174°.

misconceptions.A: This is 10° short. The complement is 42° and the supplement is 132°. Add them again.
misconceptions.B: Check both subtractions: 90° − 48° = 42° and 180° − 48° = 132°. Then add them.
misconceptions.C: Find both angles first: the complement is 42° and the supplement is 132°. Then add the two.
misconceptions.D: Yes! The complement is 42°, the supplement is 132°, and 42° + 132° = 174°.

questionText: Angle between hour and minute hand at 7:20 pm?
hints: This is a clock angle problem. The clock face has 12 equal gaps between the numbers, and the hour hand keeps moving slowly as the minutes pass.
A full turn is 360°, so each gap between two numbers is 30°. At 20 minutes the minute hand points at 4. Now think about where the hour hand is: it has moved past 7.
Similar example: at 3:30 the minute hand is at 6. The hour hand is halfway between 3 and 4, so it is 15° before 4. From 4 to 6 is 2 gaps, which is 60°. The angle is 60° + 15° = 75°.

stepByStep.text: Each gap between two numbers on a clock is 30°.
At 20 minutes past, the minute hand points at 4. From 4 to 7 is 3 gaps.
20 minutes is one third of an hour, so the hour hand has moved one third of a gap past 7.
Add the two parts.
The angle between the hands is 100°.

misconceptions.A: This is the angle from 4 to 7. The hour hand has moved a little past 7 in 20 minutes, so add that bit.
misconceptions.B: This adds too much for the hour hand. In 20 minutes it moves one third of a 30° gap, which is 10°.
misconceptions.C: Yes! From 4 to 7 is 90°, and the hour hand is 10° past 7, so the angle is 100°.
misconceptions.D: Count the gaps from 4 to 7 first: 3 gaps of 30°. Then add the small bit the hour hand has moved past 7.

questionText: Man walking south-west turns clockwise to face north. Degrees turned?
hints: This is a turning problem on the compass. Between two neighbouring directions, such as north and north-east, the turn is 45°.
Start at south-west and move clockwise. Name each direction you pass until you reach north, and count the 45° steps.

Similar example: a boy faces north-east and turns clockwise to face north-west. He passes east, south-east, south, south-west, west and then north-west. That is 6 steps of 45°, so he turns 6 × 45° = 270°.

stepByStep.text: The eight compass directions are 45° apart.
Clockwise from south-west he passes west, then north-west, then north. That is 3 steps.
Each step is 45°.
135° is not in the list, so the answer is None of these.

misconceptions.A: 90° clockwise from south-west reaches north-west. He has to go one more step to reach north.
misconceptions.B: 225° is the turn the other way round, anticlockwise. Clockwise it is shorter.
misconceptions.C: A turn of 180° from south-west ends at north-east, the opposite direction.
misconceptions.D: Yes! The turn is 3 steps of 45°, which is 135°, and that is not one of the listed values.

questionText: Angle between hour and minute at 18 minutes past 5?
hints: This is a clock angle problem. Measure each hand's turn from the 12, and remember the hour hand keeps moving as the minutes pass.
The minute hand turns 6° every minute. Find how far it has turned from 12 in 18 minutes. Then find where the hour hand is.

Similar example: at 10 minutes past 4, the minute hand has turned 10 × 6° = 60° from 12. The hour hand has turned 4 × 30° = 120°, plus 5° more for the 10 minutes, so it is at 125°. The angle between them is 125° − 60° = 65°.

stepByStep.text: The minute hand turns 6° each minute. In 18 minutes it is 108° from 12.
At 5 o'clock the hour hand is 150° from 12.
The hour hand moves 1° every 2 minutes, so in 18 minutes it moves 9° more.
Subtract to find the angle between the hands.
The angle is 51°.

misconceptions.A: Yes! The hour hand is at 159° and the minute hand at 108°, and 159° − 108° = 51°.
misconceptions.B: Check the hour hand. It starts at 150° and moves 9° more in 18 minutes, so it is at 159°. Then subtract 108°.
misconceptions.C: Check the minute hand. It turns 6° each minute, so 18 minutes is 108° from 12.
misconceptions.D: Check the subtraction: the hour hand is at 159° and the minute hand is at 108°.

questionText: Which pair of angles is supplementary?
hints: This is about supplementary angles. Two angles are supplementary when they add up to exactly 180°.
Add the two angles in each pair. Start with 62° + 128° and see whether it makes 180°.
Similar example: is 112.5° and 67.5° a supplementary pair? Add them: 112.5 + 67.5 = 180. Yes, they are supplementary. Is 95° and 75°? 95 + 75 = 170, so that pair is not.

stepByStep.text: Supplementary angles add up to 180°, so add each pair.
Add the first pair.
Add the second pair.
Add the third pair.
Add the fourth pair.
Only the last pair makes 180°. The supplementary pair is 140.5° & 39.5°.

misconceptions.B: 73.5° + 107.5° = 181°. That is just 1° too much.
misconceptions.D: Yes! 140.5° + 39.5° = 180°, so this pair is supplementary.

questionText: A line segment has how many end points?
hints: This is about the parts of a line. Think about the difference between a line, a ray and a line segment.
A line segment is a piece of a line that starts at one point and stops at another. Count the points where it stops.
Similar example: how many end points does a ray have? A ray starts at one point and goes on forever in one direction. So a ray has 1 end point.

stepByStep.text: A line segment is a straight path between two points.
It stops at both of those points, so each one is an end point.
A line segment has 2 end points.

misconceptions.A: Yes! A line segment stops at both sides, so it has 2 end points.
misconceptions.B: One end point describes a ray, which goes on forever on one side. A line segment stops at both sides.
misconceptions.C: No end points describes a line, which goes on forever both ways. A line segment stops at both sides.
misconceptions.D: A line segment has endless points on it, but it only stops at its two ends.

questionText: How many lines can pass through two distinct points?
hints: This is about lines and points. Picture two dots on paper and a ruler.
Mark two different points and lay a ruler so its edge touches both. Try to draw a second, different straight line through both.
Similar example: how many lines can pass through a single point? You can keep turning a ruler around that point and draw a new line each time. So endless lines pass through a single point.

stepByStep.text: Mark two different points and join them with a ruler. You get a straight line.
Any other straight line through both points lies exactly on top of the first.
So only One line can pass through two distinct points.

misconceptions.A: Yes! Two points fix the line completely, so there is exactly one.
misconceptions.B: Try drawing a second straight line through both points. It falls exactly on the first one.
misconceptions.C: Endless lines pass through a single point. Once a second point is fixed, the line cannot turn any more.
misconceptions.D: You can always join two points with a ruler, so there is a line.

questionText: Three or more points on the same line are called:
hints: This is a geometry word question. Think about what the parts of each word mean.
'Co' means together, as in co-operate. Look for the word that means together on one line.
Similar example: three or more lines that pass through the same point are called concurrent lines. The word tells you they run together through one point.

stepByStep.text: 'Co' means together and 'linear' means on a line.
So points that lie together on the same line are called collinear points.
Three or more points on the same line are called Collinear.

misconceptions.A: Yes! Collinear means lying together on the same line.
misconceptions.B: Non-collinear means the points do not all lie on one line. Here they do.
misconceptions.C: Concurrent is used for lines that meet at one point. Here we are naming points on one line.
misconceptions.D: Parallel is used for lines that never meet. Here we are naming points on one line.

questionText: An angle less than 90° is called:
hints: This is about naming angles by size. Each name goes with a range of degrees, measured against 90° and 180°.
Compare with a right angle, which is exactly 90°. Which name is used for an angle smaller than that?
Similar example: an angle more than 90° but less than 180° is called an obtuse angle. For example, 120° is obtuse.

stepByStep.text: A right angle is exactly 90°.
An angle smaller than a right angle, between 0° and 90°, has its own name.
An angle less than 90° is called an Acute angle.

misconceptions.A: Yes! Acute angles are the ones smaller than 90°.
misconceptions.B: A right angle is exactly 90°, not less.
misconceptions.C: An obtuse angle is more than 90°. Here the angle is less than 90°.
misconceptions.D: A straight angle is 180°, a straight line. Here the angle is less than 90°.

questionText: A right angle measures:
hints: This is about the size of a special angle. Think of the corner of a square or of your book.
A full turn is 360°. A right angle is a quarter of a full turn.
Similar example: a straight angle is half of a full turn. Half of 360° is 360° ÷ 2 = 180°, so a straight angle measures 180°.

stepByStep.text: A full turn is 360°. A right angle is a quarter turn, like the corner of a square.
Divide the full turn into 4 equal parts.
A right angle measures 90°.

misconceptions.A: Yes! A right angle is a quarter turn, and a quarter of 360° is 90°.
misconceptions.B: 180° is a straight angle, which is two right angles together.
misconceptions.C: 45° is half of a right angle.
misconceptions.D: 360° is a full turn, which is four right angles.

questionText: An angle of 180° is called a:
hints: This is about naming angles by size. Picture what the two arms of the angle look like.
Draw an angle of 180°. The two arms point in opposite directions. What shape do they make together?
Similar example: an angle of 360° is a full turn back to the start, so it is called a complete angle.

stepByStep.text: 180° is half of a full turn.
The two arms point in opposite directions and form a straight line.
So an angle of 180° is called a Straight angle.

misconceptions.A: Yes! At 180° the two arms form a straight line.
misconceptions.B: A right angle is 90°, half of 180°.
misconceptions.C: A reflex angle is more than 180° and less than 360°.
misconceptions.D: A complete angle is a full turn of 360°.

questionText: What type of angle is 135°?
hints: This is about naming an angle by its size. Compare the angle with 90° and with 180°.
Is 135° more than 90°? Is it less than 180°? Use both answers to pick the name.
Similar example: what type of angle is 200°? It is more than 180° and less than 360°, so it is a reflex angle.

stepByStep.text: 135° is more than 90°, so it is bigger than a right angle.
135° is less than 180°, so it is smaller than a straight angle.
An angle between 90° and 180° is obtuse. So 135° is an Obtuse angle.

misconceptions.A: Yes! 135° lies between 90° and 180°, so it is obtuse.
misconceptions.B: An acute angle is less than 90°. 135° is more than 90°.
misconceptions.C: A right angle is exactly 90°. 135° is bigger.
misconceptions.D: A reflex angle is more than 180°. 135° is less than 180°.

questionText: Two angles that add up to 90° are called:
hints: This is a geometry word question about pairs of angles. Two special totals have their own names: 90° and 180°.
One name is for pairs that make a right angle, the other for pairs that make a straight line. Decide which total 90° is.
Similar example: 110° and 70° add up to 180°. Two angles that add up to 180° are called supplementary angles.

stepByStep.text: Two angles that add up to 90° make a right angle together.
For example, 30° and 60°.
Such a pair of angles is called Complementary.

misconceptions.A: Yes! Angles that add up to 90° are complementary.
misconceptions.B: Supplementary angles add up to 180°. A total of 90° has a different name.
misconceptions.C: Adjacent angles sit next to each other and share an arm. They can add up to any total.
misconceptions.D: Vertically opposite angles are formed where two lines cross, and they are equal. The name for a total of 90° is different.

questionText: Three angles lie side by side on a straight line. Two of them are 48° and 67°. What is the third angle?
hints: Angles that lie side by side on a straight line add up to a straight angle. Remember how many degrees that is.
A straight angle is 180°. Add the two angles you know, then see what is left.
A similar one: two angles of 50° and 70° on a straight line make 120° together, so the third angle is 180° − 120° = 60°.

stepByStep.text: Angles on a straight line add up to 180°.
Add the two known angles.
Take this away from 180°.
The third angle is 65°.

misconceptions.A: 115° is the two known angles added together. Take that away from 180° to find the third.
misconceptions.C: 245° comes from using 360°. That is for angles all the way around a point. On a straight line the total is 180°.
misconceptions.D: 75° comes from a slip in the subtraction. Check it by adding: 115 + 65 = 180.

questionText: A round pizza is cut from the centre into 8 equal slices. Ria eats 3 slices. What angle at the centre do the remaining slices make together?
hints: The angles all the way around a point add up to 360°. Equal slices share this equally.
Find the angle of one slice by sharing 360° among 8 slices. Then count the slices that are left.
A similar one: a cake cut into 6 equal slices has 360° ÷ 6 = 60° in each slice. If 2 are eaten, the 4 left make 4 × 60° = 240°.

stepByStep.text: The angle at the centre of one slice.
Slices left.
Angle made by the slices left.
The remaining slices make an angle of 225°.

misconceptions.A: 135° is the angle of the 3 slices Ria ate. The question asks about the slices that are left.
misconceptions.B: 45° is the angle of one slice. Five slices are left.
misconceptions.C: Yes! Five slices of 45° each make 225°.
misconceptions.D: 315° is what is left after only one slice is eaten. Ria ate 3 slices.

questionText: Through how many degrees does the hour hand of a clock turn between 3 p.m. and 7:30 p.m. on the same day?
hints: The hour hand goes once around the clock, 360°, in 12 hours. Find how far it turns in one hour.
In one hour the hour hand turns 360° ÷ 12 = 30°. How many hours are there from 3 p.m. to 7:30 p.m.?
A similar one: from 1 p.m. to 3:30 p.m. is 2 and a half hours. The hour hand turns 30° + 30° for the two hours and 15° for the half hour, which is 75°.

stepByStep.text: The hour hand turns 30° every hour.
From 3 p.m. to 7:30 p.m. is 4 and a half hours.
Four hours give 120°, and half an hour gives half of 30°, which is 15°.
The hour hand turns through 135°.

misconceptions.A: Yes! 120° for the four hours and 15° more for the half hour make 135°.
misconceptions.B: 120° is the turn for 4 hours. The hour hand keeps moving during the extra half hour.
misconceptions.C: 270° uses 60° for each hour. The hour hand moves only 30° in an hour.
misconceptions.D: 150° is the turn for 5 full hours. The time from 3 p.m. to 7:30 p.m. is 4 and a half hours.

questionText: Arjun is facing East. He makes a three-quarter turn anticlockwise. Which direction is he facing now?
hints: A quarter turn is 90° and takes you from one main direction to the next. Anticlockwise is the opposite way to the hands of a clock.
Starting from East, one quarter turn anticlockwise brings Arjun to North. Make two more quarter turns the same way.
A similar one: facing North, a half turn anticlockwise goes North to West to South. So that person ends up facing South.

stepByStep.text: Going anticlockwise, the directions come in the order East, North, West, South.
First quarter turn: East to North. Second quarter turn: North to West.
Third quarter turn: West to South.
Arjun is now facing South.

misconceptions.A: North is where Arjun faces after one quarter turn. He makes three quarter turns.
misconceptions.B: West is where Arjun faces after a half turn. One more quarter turn is still to come.
misconceptions.C: He would face East again only after a full turn. Three quarters is one quarter short of that.
misconceptions.D: Yes! East to North to West to South is three quarter turns anticlockwise.

questionText: A ladder leans against an upright wall on level ground. The ladder makes an angle of 58° with the ground. What angle does the ladder make with the wall?
hints: The ladder, the wall and the ground make a triangle. An upright wall meets level ground at a right angle.
One angle of the triangle is 90°, so the other two angles together make 90°. One of them is 58°.
A similar one: a ladder that makes 65° with the ground makes 90° − 65° = 25° with the wall.

stepByStep.text: The wall and the ground meet at 90°. The three angles of the triangle add up to 180°.
So the two angles at the ends of the ladder add up to 90°.
Take away the angle with the ground.
The ladder makes an angle of 32° with the wall.

misconceptions.A: 122° comes from taking 58° from 180°. The right angle between the wall and the ground uses up 90° of that.
misconceptions.B: Yes! 58° and 32° make 90° together, and the third angle is the right angle.
misconceptions.C: 42° comes from a slip in the subtraction. Check it by adding: 58 + 32 = 90.
misconceptions.D: 58° is the angle with the ground. The two angles would be equal only if each were 45°.

questionText: At 6:00 the hands of a clock make an angle of 180°. By how many degrees has the angle between the hands become smaller at 6:30?
hints: Both hands move. In half an hour the minute hand goes halfway around, and the hour hand moves a little too.
At 6:30 the minute hand points at 6. The hour hand is not at 6 any more: it is halfway between 6 and 7. How many degrees is half of one hour space?
A similar one: at 3:00 the angle is 90°. At 3:30 the minute hand is at 6 and the hour hand is halfway between 3 and 4, so the angle is 90° − 15° = 75°. The angle became smaller by 15°.

stepByStep.text: At 6:30 the minute hand points exactly at 6.
The hour hand has moved halfway from 6 to 7. One hour space is 30°, so half of it is 15°.
So the angle between the hands at 6:30 is 15°.
Compare with the angle at 6:00.
The angle has become smaller by 165°.

misconceptions.A: 180° would be right if the hands were together at 6:30. The hour hand has moved on, halfway towards 7.
misconceptions.B: 150° allows a whole hour space of 30° between the hands. In half an hour the hour hand moves only half a space, 15°.
misconceptions.C: Yes! The angle goes from 180° down to 15°, which is 165° smaller.
misconceptions.D: 15° is the angle between the hands at 6:30. The question asks how much smaller it is than 180°.

questionText: The lamp of a lighthouse turns at a steady speed and makes one full turn every 40 seconds. Through how many degrees does it turn in 15 seconds?
hints: One full turn is 360°. Find how many degrees the lamp turns in one second, then in the number of seconds asked.
Share 360° equally among 40 seconds to get the turn in one second.
A similar one: a wheel makes a full turn in 20 seconds, so it turns 360° ÷ 20 = 18° each second. In 5 seconds it turns 5 × 18° = 90°.

stepByStep.text: A full turn is 360°. Find the turn in one second.
Multiply by 15 seconds.
The lamp turns through 135°.

misconceptions.A: Yes! The lamp turns 9° each second, and 15 × 9 = 135.
misconceptions.B: 150° uses 10° for each second. Share 360° among 40 seconds: it is 9° each second.
misconceptions.C: 24° comes from dividing 360° by 15. Divide by 40 first, because the full turn takes 40 seconds.
misconceptions.D: 600 comes from multiplying 15 by 40. In 15 seconds the lamp makes less than half a turn, so the result must be less than 180°.

questionText: The supplement of an angle is 3 times its complement. What is the angle?
hints: The complement of an angle is what must be added to make 90°. The supplement is what must be added to make 180°. You can test each choice.
The supplement is always 90° more than the complement. If the supplement is 3 times the complement, then that extra 90° is 2 times the complement.
A similar one: the supplement of an angle is 7 times its complement. Try 75°: its supplement is 105° and its complement is 15°, and 105 = 7 × 15. So that angle is 75°.

stepByStep.text: The supplement is 90° more than the complement, because 180° is 90° more than 90°.
The supplement is 3 times the complement, so the extra 90° is 2 times the complement.
The complement is 45°, so find the angle.
Check: the supplement is 135°, which is 3 times 45°. The angle is 45°.

misconceptions.A: For 60° the supplement is 120° and the complement is 30°. That is 4 times, not 3 times.
misconceptions.B: For 30° the supplement is 150° and the complement is 60°. That is less than 3 times.
misconceptions.C: 135° is the supplement of the angle we want. An angle bigger than 90° has no complement at all.
misconceptions.D: Yes! The supplement of 45° is 135° and its complement is 45°, and 135 = 3 × 45.

questionText: Two straight lines cross each other. One of the angles formed is 4 times the angle beside it. What is the largest angle formed?
hints: When two straight lines cross, two angles that are beside each other lie on a straight line, so they add up to 180°.
Think of the smaller angle as 1 part and the angle beside it as 4 parts. Together the 5 parts make 180°.
A similar one: if one angle is twice the angle beside it, then 3 parts make 180°. One part is 60°, so the angles are 60° and 120°, and the largest is 120°.

stepByStep.text: Two angles beside each other on a straight line add up to 180°.
The angles are 1 part and 4 parts, which is 5 parts in all.
The larger angle is 4 parts.
The largest angle formed is 144°.

misconceptions.A: 36° is the smaller angle. The angle beside it is 4 times as big.
misconceptions.B: Yes! 36° and 144° lie on a straight line and add up to 180°.
misconceptions.C: 72° shares the whole turn of 360° into 5 parts. The two angles beside each other share 180°.
misconceptions.D: 288° uses 360° for the two angles. Two angles beside each other on a straight line add up to 180°.

questionText: Five angles meet at a point and fill the whole turn around it. One of them is 80° and the other four are equal. How big is each of the four equal angles?
hints: Angles that fill the whole turn around a point add up to 360°. Take away the angle you know, then share the rest.
Take 80° away from 360°. What is left is shared equally among the four equal angles.
A similar one: four angles fill the turn around a point. One is 60° and the other three are equal. They share 360° − 60° = 300°, so each is 100°.

stepByStep.text: Angles around a point add up to 360°. Take away the known angle.
Share the rest equally among the four angles.
Each of the four equal angles is 70°.

misconceptions.A: 25° uses 180° as the total. Angles all the way around a point add up to 360°.
misconceptions.B: 56° shares 280° among five angles. Only four angles are equal, and the 80° angle has been taken out already.
misconceptions.D: 280° is the four equal angles together. Share it among the four.

questionText: What is the smaller angle between the hour hand and the minute hand of a clock at 2:40?
hints: At 2:40 the hour hand is not pointing exactly at the 2. It has been moving all the time since 2 o'clock.
The minute hand is on the 8. The hour hand moves 30° in a whole hour, so work out how far it moves in 40 minutes, which is two thirds of an hour.

Similar problem: at 4:20 the minute hand is on the 4, which is 120° from the 12. The hour hand has moved one third of 30°, which is 10°, past the 4, so it is 130° from the 12. The angle between the hands is 130 - 120 = 10°.

stepByStep.text: The minute hand is on the 8. Each number on the clock is 30° from the next.
The hour hand moves 30° in 60 minutes, so in 40 minutes it moves 20°.
So the hour hand is 20° past the 2.
Subtract to find the angle between the hands.
So the smaller angle between the hands is 160°.

misconceptions.A: Well done! The minute hand is at 240° and the hour hand at 80°, so the angle is 160°.
misconceptions.B: This keeps the hour hand exactly on the 2. By 2:40 it has moved two thirds of the way towards the 3.
misconceptions.C: This is the angle measured the long way round. The question asks for the smaller angle.
misconceptions.D: The hour hand moves 30° in an hour, so in 40 minutes it moves 20°, not 10°. Try once more.

questionText: From 2:10 to 2:50 on the same afternoon, both hands of a clock keep turning. How many more degrees does the minute hand turn than the hour hand in this time?
hints: Both hands move during this time, one fast and one slowly. Find how far each one turns, then compare.
From 2:10 to 2:50 is 40 minutes. The minute hand turns 6° every minute. The hour hand turns 30° in a whole hour.
Similar problem: from 5:00 to 5:30. The minute hand turns half a full turn, 180°. The hour hand turns half of 30°, which is 15°. The minute hand turns 180 - 15 = 165° more.

stepByStep.text: Find the time that passes.
The minute hand turns 6° each minute.
The hour hand turns 30° in 60 minutes, so 1° every 2 minutes.
Find how much more the minute hand turns.
So the minute hand turns 220° more than the hour hand.

misconceptions.A: This is how far the minute hand turns. The hour hand has also turned a little in 40 minutes. Take its turn away.
misconceptions.B: This adds the two turns. 'How many more' asks for the difference between them.
misconceptions.C: Great job! The minute hand turns 240°, the hour hand 20°, and 240 - 20 = 220.
misconceptions.D: This is how far the hour hand turns. Compare it with the turn of the minute hand.

questionText: At 12 noon the hour hand of a clock points straight up at the 12. Later the same afternoon, the hour hand has turned through exactly 75° from that position. What time is it?
hints: Work backwards from the angle. Think about how many degrees the hour hand turns in one hour, and be careful when you change a part of an hour into minutes.
The hour hand turns 30° every hour. Find how many 30s there are in 75, and what is left over.
Similar problem: the hour hand has turned 105° since noon. Three hours take 90°, and 15° are left. Since 15° is half of 30°, that is half an hour, or 30 minutes. The time is 3:30 pm.

stepByStep.text: The hour hand turns 30° in one hour.
Two hours take 60° of the turn. Find what is left.
15° is half of 30°, so it takes half an hour.
So 2 hours and 30 minutes have passed since noon.
So the time is 2:30 pm.

misconceptions.A: 75 ÷ 30 is 2 and a half hours. Half an hour is 30 minutes, not 50 minutes.
misconceptions.B: Yes! Two hours use 60°, the last 15° is half an hour, so it is 2:30 pm.
misconceptions.C: This treats 75° as 75 minutes. The hour hand is slow: it turns only 30° in a whole hour.
misconceptions.D: Two full hours use 60°. The remaining 15° is half of an hour's turn, which is much more than 5 minutes.

questionText: At 12:20, Sana says: "The minute hand is on the 4 and the hour hand is on the 12, so the angle between the hands is 120°." By how many degrees is Sana's answer different from the true angle between the hands?
hints: Check each part of what Sana says. Is each hand exactly where she says it is at 12:20?
The minute hand is exactly on the 4. Now think about the hour hand: 20 minutes is one third of an hour, and the hour hand moves 30° in an hour.
Similar problem: at 12:30 someone says the angle is 180°. But the hour hand has moved half of 30°, which is 15°, past the 12. The true angle is 180 - 15 = 165°, so that answer is 15° too big.

stepByStep.text: The minute hand is on the 4, so it is 120° from the 12.
In 20 minutes the hour hand has moved one third of 30° past the 12.
The true angle between the hands is smaller than Sana's.
Compare Sana's answer with the true angle.
So Sana's answer is different from the true angle by 10°.

misconceptions.A: Wonderful! The hour hand has crept 10° past the 12, so the true angle is 110° and Sana is 10° out.
misconceptions.B: Sana's idea sounds right, but the hour hand does not stay on the 12. In 20 minutes it moves a little towards the 1.
misconceptions.C: The hour hand moves 30° in a whole hour. In 20 minutes it moves one third of that.
misconceptions.D: 110° is the true angle between the hands. The question asks how far Sana's answer is from it.

questionText: Farhan is facing North-East. He turns 90° clockwise, then 225° anticlockwise, and then 135° clockwise. Which direction is he facing now?
hints: Follow the turns one at a time and keep track of the direction after each turn. Watch which way each turn goes.
The eight compass directions are 45° apart. A turn of 90° clockwise from North-East moves two directions on: find where that is first.

Similar problem: Asha faces North, turns 90° clockwise and then 135° anticlockwise. After the first turn she faces East. Going back 135° is three steps of 45°: North-East, North, North-West. She faces North-West.

stepByStep.text: From North-East, a 90° clockwise turn moves two steps of 45°: he faces South-East.
225° is five steps of 45°.
Five steps anticlockwise from South-East go East, North-East, North, North-West, West: he faces West.
135° is three steps of 45°.
Three steps clockwise from West go North-West, North, North-East.
So Farhan is facing North-East, the direction he started in.

misconceptions.A: This takes all three turns clockwise. The middle turn of 225° goes anticlockwise, the other way.
misconceptions.B: West is where he faces after the second turn. There is still a 135° clockwise turn to make.
misconceptions.C: Check the first two turns: the 90° turn is clockwise and the 225° turn is anticlockwise, not the other way round.
misconceptions.D: Well done! The turns take him to South-East, then West, then back to North-East.

questionText: Ravi turns 135° clockwise and then 90° anticlockwise. Now he is facing South. Which direction was he facing before he turned?
hints: You know where Ravi ends, not where he starts. To go back in time, undo each turn by turning the opposite way.
Start from South. The last thing Ravi did was turn 90° anticlockwise, so undo it first by turning 90° clockwise.
Similar problem: after turning 90° clockwise, Asha faces West. To undo this, turn 90° anticlockwise from West, which gives South. So Asha was facing South at the start.

stepByStep.text: Start from where Ravi ends: South.
Undo the last turn. It was 90° anticlockwise, so turn 90° clockwise from South: West.
Undo the first turn. It was 135° clockwise, so turn 135° anticlockwise from West: South-West, South, South-East.
Check forwards: from South-East, 135° clockwise is West, and then 90° anticlockwise is South.
So Ravi was facing South-East before he turned.

misconceptions.A: This makes the two turns again, starting from South. South is where Ravi ends, so the turns must be undone instead.
misconceptions.B: Yes! From South-East, 135° clockwise reaches West, and 90° anticlockwise from West reaches South.
misconceptions.C: West is where Ravi was facing between the two turns. Undo the first turn as well.
misconceptions.D: Each turn must be undone in the opposite direction. Check: starting from North-West, where would the two turns take him?

questionText: A toy robot is facing North. Each time Kavya presses a button, the robot turns 45° clockwise. Which direction is the robot facing after Kavya has pressed the button 13 times?
hints: The robot keeps going round and round. Look for the number of presses that brings it back to where it started.
A full turn is 360°. Find how many presses of 45° make a full turn, and then how many presses are left over after that.

Similar problem: a robot facing North turns 90° clockwise at each press. Four presses make a full turn. After 10 presses, 8 presses make two full turns and 2 are left, so it faces East and then South. It ends facing South.

stepByStep.text: Find how many presses make one full turn.
After 8 presses the robot is facing North again.
Find how many presses are left.
Five more presses from North go North-East, East, South-East, South, South-West.
So the robot is facing South-West.

misconceptions.A: So close! After the first press the robot already faces North-East. North is where it starts, before any press.
misconceptions.B: Great thinking! Eight presses bring it back to North, and five more take it to South-West.
misconceptions.C: This is one press too many. Count again: 8 presses for the full turn, then 5 more.
misconceptions.D: This is where the robot faces after 1 press. A full turn takes 8 presses, not 12, so 5 presses are left over.

questionText: Three angles meet at a point and together fill the whole turn around the point, with no gaps and no overlaps. The second angle is twice the first, and the third angle is three times the first. What kind of angle is the largest of the three?
hints: First decide what the three angles add up to. Read carefully: do they lie on a straight line, inside a triangle, or all the way round a point?
Call the first angle one part. Then the three angles are 1 part, 2 parts and 3 parts. Find how many parts there are in the whole turn.

Similar problem: two angles fill the whole turn around a point, and one is 3 times the other. There are 4 parts in 360°, so one part is 90°. The angles are 90° and 270°, and the larger one is a reflex angle.

stepByStep.text: Angles that fill the whole turn around a point add up to 360°.
The angles are 1 part, 2 parts and 3 parts, which is 6 parts.
The largest angle is 3 parts.
An angle of 180° makes a straight line.
So the largest angle is a straight angle.

misconceptions.A: This comes from a total of 180°. These angles go all the way round the point, so they add up to 360°.
misconceptions.B: The second angle, 120°, is obtuse. The question asks about the largest of the three.
misconceptions.C: Excellent! The angles are 60°, 120° and 180°, and 180° is a straight angle.
misconceptions.D: A reflex angle is more than 180°. Work out the largest angle exactly: is it more than 180°?

questionText: Two straight lines cross each other and make four angles around the crossing point. Three of these angles add up to 250°. What is the size of the smallest of the four angles?
hints: The four angles go all the way round the point. Find the angle that was left out, then use what you know about the angles made when two straight lines cross.
Take 250° away from the whole turn to find the fourth angle. The angle beside it lies with it on a straight line.
Similar problem: three of the four angles add up to 300°. The fourth is 360 - 300 = 60°. The angle beside it is 180 - 60 = 120°. The four angles are 60°, 120°, 60°, 120°, so the largest is 120°.

stepByStep.text: The four angles add up to a whole turn, so find the fourth angle.
The angle beside it makes a straight line with it.
Angles opposite each other are equal, so the four angles are 110°, 70°, 110° and 70°.
Check the three that were added.
So the smallest of the four angles is 70°.

misconceptions.A: Well done! The four angles are 110°, 70°, 110° and 70°, so the smallest is 70°.
misconceptions.B: 110° is the fourth angle, the one left out of the total. Now find the angle beside it on the straight line.
misconceptions.C: This halves the fourth angle. The angle beside 110° on a straight line is what is left from 180°.
misconceptions.D: This halves 70°. The angles around the crossing point come in two equal pairs, 110° and 70°.

questionText: An angle is 30° more than its complement. What is the supplement of this angle?
hints: There are two different ideas here, complement and supplement. Find the angle first using its complement, and then answer what is asked.
The angle and its complement add up to 90°, and the angle is 30° bigger. Take the extra 30° away from 90° and share what is left equally.
Similar problem: an angle is 10° more than its complement. Taking 10 from 90 leaves 80, so the complement is 40° and the angle is 50°. The supplement of the angle is 180 - 50 = 130°.

stepByStep.text: The angle and its complement add up to 90°. Take away the extra 30° and halve.
The complement is 30°, so the angle is 30° more.
The supplement is what the angle needs to make 180°.
So the supplement of the angle is 120°.

misconceptions.A: 60° is the angle itself. The question asks for its supplement, the angle that goes with it to make 180°.
misconceptions.B: 30° is the complement of the angle. Find the angle, and then find its supplement.
misconceptions.C: This is the supplement of 30°, which is the complement. Use the angle itself, which is 60°.
misconceptions.D: Lovely! The angle is 60°, and 180 - 60 = 120.

questionText: Angle P and angle Q are complementary, so they add up to 90°. Angle Q and angle R are supplementary, so they add up to 180°. Which of these is true whatever the size of angle P?

options.text: Angle R is equal to angle P
Angle P and angle R are supplementary
Angle R is 90° more than angle P
Angle R is twice angle Q

hints: No sizes are given, so the statement must hold for every possible angle P. Try one size for angle P, and then try a different size to make sure.
Let angle P be 20°. Find angle Q from the first clue and angle R from the second clue. Then do the same again with angle P as 40°.

Similar problem: angle X and angle Y add up to 180°, and angle Y and angle Z also add up to 180°. If X is 50°, Y is 130° and Z is 50°. If X is 70°, Y is 110° and Z is 70°. Whatever X is, Z is equal to X.

stepByStep.text: Try angle P = 20°. Then angle Q is 70° and angle R is 110°.
Try angle P = 40°. Then angle Q is 50° and angle R is 130°.
Both times angle R is 90° more than angle P.
This always happens: going from 90° to 180° adds 90° to the total, and angle Q is the same in both.
So angle R is 90° more than angle P.

misconceptions.A: Try angle P = 20°: angle Q is 70° and angle R is 110°. Angle R is much bigger than angle P.
misconceptions.B: This is true only when angle P is 45°. Try angle P = 20°: angle R is 110°, and 20 + 110 is not 180.
misconceptions.C: Well reasoned! Whatever angle P is, angle R is always 90° more.
misconceptions.D: This is true when angle P is 30°, but try another size. With angle P = 20°, angle Q is 70° and angle R is 110°, which is not twice 70°.

questionText: Angle AOB is 70°. A ray OC is drawn from the same point O so that angle BOC is 30°. Riya says angle AOC must be 100°. Which of these is true about angle AOC?

options.text: It could be any angle from 40° to 100°

hints: There is no picture, so imagine it. The ray OC can be drawn on either side of the ray OB.
First picture OC on the far side of OB, away from OA. Then picture OC on the near side of OB, between OA and OB. Find angle AOC each time.

Similar problem: angle XOY is 50° and angle YOZ is 20°. If OZ is outside angle XOY, angle XOZ is 50 + 20 = 70°. If OZ is inside angle XOY, angle XOZ is 50 - 20 = 30°. So angle XOZ could be 70° or 30°.

stepByStep.text: The ray OC makes 30° with OB, and it can lie on either side of OB.
If OC is on the side away from OA, the two angles add.
If OC is between OA and OB, the smaller angle is taken away.
These are the only two places where OC can be.
So angle AOC could be 100° or 40°.

misconceptions.A: Riya has added the angles, which is right if OC is outside angle AOB. But OC could also be drawn between OA and OB.
misconceptions.B: 40° is right if OC lies between OA and OB. But OC could also be on the other side of OB.
misconceptions.C: Angle BOC is fixed at 30°, so OC has only two possible places, one on each side of OB. It cannot be anywhere in between.
misconceptions.D: Great thinking! OC can be on either side of OB, giving 70 + 30 = 100 or 70 - 30 = 40.

questionText: Two angles are supplementary. If one angle is 89°, find the other.
hints: This is about supplementary angles. Two angles are supplementary when together they make a straight line.
Supplementary angles add up to 180°. One of them is 89°, so think about how much more is needed to reach 180°.
Similar example: if one angle is 110°, its supplement is 180° − 110° = 70°. Check: 110° + 70° = 180°.

stepByStep.text: Two supplementary angles make a straight line together, and a straight line is 180°.
One angle is 89°, so take 89 away from 180: 180 − 89 = 91.
Check by adding: 89° + 91° = 180°. The other angle is 91°.

misconceptions.A: 271 is 360 − 89, which uses a full turn. Here the two angles together make only 180°.
misconceptions.B: 89° is the angle you were given. The other angle is what must be added to it to make 180°.
misconceptions.C: 1 is 90 − 89. These two angles add up to 180°, not 90°.
misconceptions.D: That's it! The two angles must make 180° together, and 89 + 91 = 180.

questionText: Two angles are supplementary. If one angle is 71°, find the other.
hints: Supplementary angles are a pair of angles that fit together to make a straight line. Think about how big a straight angle is.
Supplementary angles add up to 180°. One of them is 71°, so think about how much more is needed to reach 180°.
Similar example: if one angle is 140°, its supplement is 180° − 140° = 40°. Check: 140° + 40° = 180°.

stepByStep.text: Supplementary angles add up to 180°.
One angle is 71°, so take 71 away from 180: 180 − 71 = 109.
Check by adding: 71° + 109° = 180°. The other angle is 109°.

misconceptions.A: That's it! The two angles must make 180° together, and 71 + 109 = 180.
misconceptions.B: 19 is 90 − 71. These two angles add up to 180°, not 90°.
misconceptions.C: 289 is 360 − 71. A full turn is 360°, but supplementary angles add up to 180°.
misconceptions.D: 71° is the first angle again. Find how much more is needed to reach 180°.

questionText: Two straight lines cross. One angle formed is 22°. Find the vertically opposite angle.
hints: When two straight lines cross they make four angles. Vertically opposite angles are the two that face each other across the crossing point.
Draw two crossing lines and mark one angle as 22°. Look at the angle straight across from it. Does it look bigger, smaller or the same?
Similar example: two straight lines cross and one angle is 145°. The angle facing it is vertically opposite, so it is 145° as well. The angles beside it are each 180° − 145° = 35°.

stepByStep.text: When two straight lines cross, the angles that face each other are called vertically opposite angles.
The angle beside the 22° angle shares a straight line with it, so it is 180 − 22 = 158°. The angle on the other side of that one is 180 − 158 = 22° again.
So vertically opposite angles are equal, and the vertically opposite angle is 22°.

misconceptions.A: 158 is 180 − 22, the angle next to it on the straight line. Look at the angle straight across instead.
misconceptions.B: 68 is 90 − 22, but nothing here makes a right angle. Picture the X the two lines make and compare the angles that face each other.
misconceptions.C: That's it! When two straight lines cross, the angles facing each other are equal, so this one is 22° too.
misconceptions.D: 338 is 360 − 22, the rest of a full turn. The vertically opposite angle is just the one facing the 22° angle.

questionText: Two angles on a straight line are x° and 56°. Find x.
hints: Two angles sit side by side on a straight line. Together they fill the whole straight line, so think about how big a straight angle is.
The two angles together make the straight line, which is 180°. One of them is 56°, so think about how much is left for x.
Similar example: if the two angles on a straight line are x° and 20°, then x = 180 − 20 = 160. Check: 160 + 20 = 180.

stepByStep.text: A straight line is an angle of 180°. The two angles, x° and 56°, share it between them.
Take 56 away from 180: 180 − 56 = 124.
Check by adding: 124 + 56 = 180. So x = 124.

misconceptions.A: 304 is 360 − 56. A full turn is 360°, but angles on a straight line add up to 180°.
misconceptions.B: Yes! Angles on a straight line add up to 180°, and 180 − 56 = 124.
misconceptions.C: 56° is the angle you were given. The other angle is what must be added to it to make 180°.
misconceptions.D: 34 is 90 − 56. These two angles add up to 180°, not 90°.

questionText: Two straight lines cross. One angle formed is 59°. Find the vertically opposite angle.

questionText: Two angles are supplementary. If one angle is 49°, find the other.
hints: This is about supplementary angles. Two angles are supplementary when together they make a straight line.
The two angles together make 180°. You know one is 49°, so the other is the rest of the 180°.
Similar example: if one angle is 125°, its supplement is 180° − 125° = 55°. Check: 125° + 55° = 180°.

stepByStep.text: Two supplementary angles make a straight line together, and a straight line is 180°.
One angle is 49°, so take 49 away from 180: 180 − 49 = 131.
Check by adding: 49° + 131° = 180°. The other angle is 131°.

misconceptions.A: 41 is 90 − 49. These two angles add up to 180°, not 90°.
misconceptions.B: Yes! Supplementary angles add up to 180°, and 180 − 49 = 131.
misconceptions.C: 49° is the angle you were given. The other angle is what must be added to it to make 180°.
misconceptions.D: 311 is 360 − 49, which uses a full turn. Here the two angles together make only 180°.

questionText: Two straight lines cross. One angle formed is 160°. Find the vertically opposite angle.
hints: When two straight lines cross they make four angles. Vertically opposite angles are the two that face each other across the crossing point.
Draw two crossing lines and mark one angle as 160°. Look at the angle straight across from it. Does it look bigger, smaller or the same?
Similar example: two straight lines cross and one angle is 40°. The angle facing it is vertically opposite, so it is 40° as well. The angles beside it are each 180° − 40° = 140°.

stepByStep.text: When two straight lines cross, the angles that face each other are called vertically opposite angles.
The angle beside the 160° angle shares a straight line with it, so it is 180 − 160 = 20°. The angle on the other side of that one is 180 − 20 = 160° again.
So vertically opposite angles are equal, and the vertically opposite angle is 160°.

misconceptions.A: That's it! When two straight lines cross, the angles facing each other are equal, so this one is 160° too.
misconceptions.B: 20 is 180 − 160, the angle next to it on the straight line. Look at the angle straight across instead.
misconceptions.C: 200 is 360 − 160. That is all the other angles at the crossing put together, but the question asks for only one of them.
misconceptions.D: 250 is much bigger than the 160° you were given. Picture the X the two lines make and compare the two angles that face each other.

questionText: Two angles on a straight line are x° and 27°. Find x.
hints: Two angles sit side by side on a straight line. Together they fill the whole straight line, so think about how big a straight angle is.
The two angles together make the straight line, which is 180°. One of them is 27°, so think about how much is left for x.
Similar example: if the two angles on a straight line are x° and 20°, then x = 180 − 20 = 160. Check: 160 + 20 = 180.

stepByStep.text: A straight line is an angle of 180°. The two angles, x° and 27°, share it between them.
Take 27 away from 180: 180 − 27 = 153.
Check by adding: 153 + 27 = 180. So x = 153.

misconceptions.A: 63 is 90 − 27. That would fit two angles making a right angle, but angles on a straight line add up to 180°.
misconceptions.B: Yes! Angles on a straight line add up to 180°, and 180 − 27 = 153.
misconceptions.C: 333 is 360 − 27, which uses a full turn. Here the two angles together make only 180°.
misconceptions.D: 27° is the first angle again. Find how much more is needed to reach 180°.

questionText: Two angles on a straight line are x° and 154°. Find x.
hints: This is about angles on a straight line. Think about what the angles on one side of a straight line add up to.

stepByStep.text: Angles on a straight line add up to 180°, so x° and 154° together make 180°.

questionText: A man was standing facing South, after a while he is seen facing the North-East direction. Which of the following statement is true in regards to his position?

options.text: He turned 45° in the clock-wise direction
He turned 135° in the anticlock-wise direction
He turned 135° in the clock-wise direction
He turned 270° in the anticlock-wise direction

hints: This is about turning between compass directions. Picture the eight directions around a compass and think about the angle between two neighbours.
The 8 directions share a full turn of 360°, so each step to the next direction is 45°. Count the steps from South to North-East, going each way round.

Similar example: a girl faces North-West and then faces South-West. Going anticlockwise she passes West and reaches South-West, which is 2 steps of 45°. 2 × 45 = 90, so she turned 90° anticlockwise. Going clockwise would take 6 steps, which is 270°.

stepByStep.text: The 8 compass directions share a full turn of 360°, so each step from one direction to the next is 45°.
Going anticlockwise from South, the man passes South-East, then East, and reaches North-East. That is 3 steps.
Three steps of 45° make 135°.
Going clockwise he would pass South-West, West, North-West and North before reaching North-East. That is 5 steps, or 225°, and none of the choices says that.
The trap is to mix up the two ways round. He turned 135° in the anticlock-wise direction.

misconceptions.A: A 45° clockwise turn from South reaches South-West, which is only one step away. North-East is further round.
misconceptions.B: Yes! From South, three steps anticlockwise pass South-East and East and reach North-East, and 3 × 45 = 135.
misconceptions.C: The size of the turn is right, but turning 135° clockwise from South reaches North-West. Check which way round leads to North-East.
misconceptions.D: A 270° anticlockwise turn from South is 6 steps, which reaches West. North-East is only 3 steps away going that way round.

questionText: Which of the following angle given below could be the supplementary angle to 57 1/4°?
hints: Supplementary angles are two angles that add up to 180°. So you need the angle that is still missing to reach 180°.
Subtract 57 1/4 from 180. It helps to take away the whole number 57 first, and then take away the extra quarter.
Similar example: the supplementary angle of 40 1/2°. First 180 − 40 = 140. Then take away the extra half, which leaves 139 1/2. So the angle is 139 1/2°.

stepByStep.text: Supplementary angles add up to 180°, so subtract 57 1/4 from 180.
Take away the whole number first.
Now take away the extra quarter. One quarter less than 123 is 122 and three quarters.
Check by adding: 57 1/4 and 122 3/4 make 180. So the supplementary angle is 122 3/4°.

misconceptions.A: Here the quarter was added back on. After 180 − 57 = 123, the quarter still has to be taken away.
misconceptions.B: The fraction is right, but the whole number is 1 too small. 180 − 57 is 123, and a quarter less than that is just under 123.
misconceptions.C: Add this to 57 1/4 and you get 178 1/2, not 180. Take 57 from 180, then take away one quarter.
misconceptions.D: Yes! 57 1/4 and 122 3/4 add up to exactly 180.

questionText: In 300 seconds the minute hand of a clock moves ______ degrees?
hints: This question mixes time and angles. Change the seconds into minutes, and think about how far the minute hand turns in a full hour.
First change 300 seconds into minutes, using 60 seconds in 1 minute. Then find how many degrees the minute hand turns in 1 minute.
Similar example: in 600 seconds, 600 ÷ 60 = 10 minutes pass. The minute hand turns 360° in 60 minutes, so it turns 360 ÷ 60 = 6° each minute. In 10 minutes it turns 10 × 6 = 60°.

stepByStep.text: Change the seconds to minutes. There are 60 seconds in a minute.
The minute hand goes once round the clock, which is 360°, in 60 minutes. So it turns 6° each minute.
In 5 minutes it turns 5 times 6°. The minute hand moves 30 degrees.

misconceptions.A: This is 5 × 30. The gap from one number on the clock to the next is 30°, and the minute hand takes the whole 5 minutes to cross one gap.
misconceptions.B: 60 is the number of seconds in a minute. 300 seconds is 5 minutes, and the minute hand turns 6° each minute.
misconceptions.C: Yes! 300 seconds is 5 minutes, and the minute hand turns 6° each minute, so 5 × 6 = 30.
misconceptions.D: This is half of the turn. In 5 minutes the minute hand moves from one number on the clock to the next, and 360 ÷ 12 gives the size of that gap.

questionText: Which of the following pairs of angles are complementary to each other?
hints: Complementary angles are two angles that add up to 90°. Test each pair by adding.
Add the two angles in the first pair and see whether the total is 90°. Do the same for each of the other pairs.
Similar example: are 35° and 55° complementary? 35 + 55 = 90, so yes. Are 50° and 50° complementary? 50 + 50 = 100, so no.

stepByStep.text: Complementary angles add up to 90°. Add each pair and compare with 90.
30° and 30° make 60°, and 40° and 30° make 70°. Both are too small.
34° and 66° make 100°, which is too big.
22 and 68 add up to 90. So the complementary pair is 22° & 68°.

misconceptions.A: 30° and 30° add up to 60°. Complementary angles must add up to 90°.
misconceptions.B: 40° and 30° add up to 70°, which is 20° short of 90°.
misconceptions.C: Yes! 22 + 68 = 90, so these two angles are complementary.
misconceptions.D: 34° and 66° add up to 100°. That is close, but complementary angles add up to exactly 90°.

questionText: An angle measures 35°. What is the sum of the complementary and the supplementary angles of the given angle?
hints: This uses two angle facts. Complementary angles add up to 90°, and supplementary angles add up to 180°.
Find the complementary angle of 35° by subtracting it from 90°. Then find its supplementary angle in the same way, using 180°.
Similar example: for an angle of 20°, the complementary angle is 90 − 20 = 70° and the supplementary angle is 180 − 20 = 160°. Their sum is 70 + 160 = 230°.

stepByStep.text: The complementary angle and 35° make 90°.
The supplementary angle and 35° make 180°.
Add the two angles you found. The sum is 200°.

misconceptions.A: Yes! The complementary angle is 55° and the supplementary angle is 145°, and 55 + 145 = 200.
misconceptions.B: Check the two subtractions, 90 − 35 and 180 − 35. Then add the two results carefully.
misconceptions.C: 180° is what an angle and its supplementary angle add up to. Here you add the complementary angle, 55°, and the supplementary angle, 145°.
misconceptions.D: Find the complementary angle, 90 − 35, and the supplementary angle, 180 − 35. Add those two, with nothing else taken away.

questionText: Which pair of angles given below are complementary to each other?
hints: This is about complementary angles. Two angles are complementary when they add up to exactly 90°.
Add the two angles in each pair. Start with 55° + 45° and see whether it makes 90°.
Similar example: is 40° and 50° a complementary pair? Add them: 40 + 50 = 90, so yes. Is 30° and 70°? 30 + 70 = 100, so that pair is not.

stepByStep.text: Complementary angles add up to 90°, so add each pair.
Add the first pair.
Add the second pair.
Add the third pair.
Add the fourth pair.
Only one pair makes 90°. The complementary pair is 65° & 25°.

misconceptions.A: 55° + 45° = 100°. That is 10° more than 90°.
misconceptions.B: Yes! 65° + 25° = 90°, so this pair is complementary.
misconceptions.C: 35° + 48° = 83°. That is less than 90°.
misconceptions.D: 17° + 63° = 80°. That is 10° short of 90°.

questionText: When a boy asks a teacher, what is the time now?, the teacher replies, the angle between the hour hand and the minute hand of my watch makes an angle of 45° now. What time is it now?
hints: This is about the angle between the hands of a clock. The 12 numbers split the clock into 12 equal gaps, and the hour hand keeps moving slowly between the numbers.
Each gap between two numbers on the clock is 360 ÷ 12 = 30°. For each time, find where the minute hand points and where the hour hand has moved to, then count the gaps between them.

Similar example: at 3:30 the minute hand is on 6 and the hour hand is halfway between 3 and 4. From there to 6 is 2 and a half gaps. Two gaps are 60° and half a gap is 15°, so the angle is 60 + 15 = 75°.

stepByStep.text: Each gap between two numbers on a clock is 30°.
An angle of 45° is 1 and a half gaps.
At half past, the minute hand is on 6 and the hour hand is halfway between two numbers. The trap is to forget that the hour hand has moved on.
At 7:30 the hour hand is halfway between 7 and 8. From 6 to 7 is one gap, and then there is half a gap more. That makes 45°.
At 2:30 there are 3 and a half gaps and at 8:30 there are 2 and a half gaps, and at 1:15 the angle is a little more than 45°. So the time is 7:30.

misconceptions.A: At 1:15 the minute hand is on 3 and the hour hand is a quarter of a gap past 1. That is 1 and three-quarter gaps, which is 52 and a half degrees.
misconceptions.B: At 2:30 the hour hand is halfway between 2 and 3 and the minute hand is on 6. That is 3 and a half gaps, which is 105°.
misconceptions.C: At 8:30 the hour hand is halfway between 8 and 9, so it is 2 and a half gaps from the 6. That is 75°, one gap too many.
misconceptions.D: Yes! At 7:30 the hour hand is halfway between 7 and 8, which is 1 and a half gaps from the 6, and that is 45°.

questionText: What is the supplement of an angle of 153°?
hints: This is about supplementary angles. Two angles are supplementary when together they make a straight line.
Supplementary angles add up to 180°. So take 153° away from 180°.
Similar example: the supplement of 70° is 180° − 70° = 110°. Check: 70° + 110° = 180°.

stepByStep.text: Supplementary angles add up to 180°.
Take the given angle away from 180°.
Check by adding: 153° + 27° = 180°. The supplement of 153° is 27°.

misconceptions.A: Yes! 153° + 27° = 180°, so the supplement is 27°.
misconceptions.B: Close, but this is 10° too big. Check the tens when you take 153° away from 180°.
misconceptions.C: Close, but this is 10° too small. Check the tens when you take 153° away from 180°.
misconceptions.D: This is too big. The two angles together make only 180°, so the supplement must be smaller than 180°.

questionText: What is the complement of an angle of 51°?
hints: This is about complementary angles. Two angles are complementary when together they make a right angle.
Complementary angles add up to 90°. So take 51° away from 90°.
Similar example: the complement of 20° is 90° − 20° = 70°. Check: 20° + 70° = 90°.

stepByStep.text: Complementary angles add up to 90°.
Take the given angle away from 90°.
Check by adding: 51° + 39° = 90°. The complement of 51° is 39°.

misconceptions.A: This is too big. The two angles together make only 90°, so the complement must be smaller than 90°.
misconceptions.B: Close, but this is 10° too big. Check the tens when you take 51° away from 90°.
misconceptions.C: Yes! 51° + 39° = 90°, so the complement is 39°.
misconceptions.D: Close, but this is 10° too small. Check the tens when you take 51° away from 90°.

questionText: What is the supplement of an angle of 95°?
hints: This is about supplementary angles. Two angles are supplementary when together they make a straight line.
Supplementary angles add up to 180°. So take 95° away from 180°.
Similar example: the supplement of 70° is 180° − 70° = 110°. Check: 70° + 110° = 180°.

stepByStep.text: Supplementary angles add up to 180°.
Take the given angle away from 180°.
Check by adding: 95° + 85° = 180°. The supplement of 95° is 85°.

misconceptions.A: This is the angle itself. The supplement is what you add to 95° to make 180°.
misconceptions.B: Close, but this is 10° too small. Check the tens when you take 95° away from 180°.
misconceptions.C: Yes! 95° + 85° = 180°, so the supplement is 85°.
misconceptions.D: This is too big. The two angles together make only 180°, so the supplement must be smaller than 180°.

questionText: What is the supplement of an angle of 125°?
hints: This is about supplementary angles. Two angles are supplementary when together they make a straight line.
Supplementary angles add up to 180°. So take 125° away from 180°.

Take the given angle away from 180°.
Check by adding: 125° + 55° = 180°. The supplement of 125° is 55°.

questionText: What is the complement of an angle of 73°?
hints: This is about complementary angles. Two angles are complementary when together they make a right angle.
Complementary angles add up to 90°. So take 73° away from 90°.
Similar example: the complement of 20° is 90° − 20° = 70°. Check: 20° + 70° = 90°.

stepByStep.text: Complementary angles add up to 90°.
Take the given angle away from 90°.
Check by adding: 73° + 17° = 90°. The complement of 73° is 17°.

misconceptions.A: Close, but this is 10° too big. Check the tens when you take 73° away from 90°.
