questionText: An angle that measures more than 90° but less than 180° is called:
hints: This question is about the names of angles. Each name goes with a size, so think about where this angle sits compared with 90° and 180°.

Picture the corner of a book, which is 90°, and a flat straight line, which is 180°. This angle is wider than the corner of the book but has not opened out flat. Which name belongs to an angle like that?
A similar example: an angle of 40° is smaller than 90°, the corner of a book. Angles smaller than 90° are called acute, so a 40° angle is an acute angle.

stepByStep.text: An angle smaller than 90° is called acute, and an angle of exactly 90° is called a right angle.
An angle bigger than 180° is called a reflex angle.
That leaves the angles in between. An angle that measures more than 90° but less than 180° is called obtuse.

misconceptions.A: Acute angles are the small, sharp ones that are less than 90°. This angle is more than 90°, so look for the name of the wider kind.
misconceptions.B: A right angle is exactly 90°, like the corner of a book. This angle is more than 90°, so it needs a different name.
misconceptions.C: Yes! An obtuse angle is wider than a right angle but has not opened out to a straight line.
misconceptions.D: A reflex angle is more than 180°, past a straight line. This angle is still less than 180°, so think of the name for angles between 90° and 180°.

questionText: An angle measuring 250° is a:
hints: This question is about the names of angles. Each name goes with a range of sizes, so think about which range this angle falls in.
Compare 250° with a straight angle, which is 180°, and with a full turn, which is 360°. Is 250° smaller than both, between them, or bigger than both?
Here is a similar one: what kind of angle is 120°? It is more than 90° and less than 180°, so 120° is an obtuse angle.

stepByStep.text: A straight angle is exactly 180° and a complete angle is exactly 360°.
250° is more than 180° but less than 360°.
An angle between 180° and 360° is called a reflex angle. So 250° is a reflex angle.

misconceptions.A: Yes! 250° is more than 180° and less than 360°, and angles in between those are reflex angles.
misconceptions.B: A straight angle is exactly 180°, a flat line. 250° has turned further than that.
misconceptions.C: An obtuse angle is between 90° and 180°. 250° is bigger than 180°, so it needs a different name.
misconceptions.D: A complete angle is a full turn of exactly 360°. 250° stops before the full turn.

questionText: Which instrument is used to measure an angle?
hints: This question is about the tools in a geometry box. Each tool has one main job, so think about what each one is used for.
Angles are measured in degrees. Think about which tool in the box has degrees, from 0° to 180°, marked around its curved edge.

A similar example: to measure how long a line is, we use a ruler, because a ruler has centimetres marked along its edge. In the same way, the tool for measuring an angle is the one with degrees marked on it.

stepByStep.text: Angles are measured in degrees, so we need a tool with degrees marked on it.
A compass draws circles, a pair of dividers compares lengths, and a set square helps draw a few fixed angles.
The half-circle tool marked from 0° to 180° is the one used to measure an angle. It is the protractor.

misconceptions.A: Yes! A protractor has degrees marked around its edge, so it can measure any angle.
misconceptions.B: A compass holds a pencil and draws circles. It has no degrees marked on it, so look for the tool that does.
misconceptions.C: A pair of dividers has two sharp points for comparing lengths. To measure an angle you need a tool marked in degrees.
misconceptions.D: A set square helps you draw a few fixed angles such as 90°, but it cannot measure any angle you like. Look for the tool with degrees marked on it.

questionText: What is the complementary angle of 67½°?
hints: This question is about complementary angles. Remember what two complementary angles add up to, and then find the missing part.
Two complementary angles add up to 90°. So take 67½° away from 90°. It is easier to take away the 67° first and the ½° after that.
A similar example: find the complementary angle of 34½°. First 90° − 34° = 56°. Then take away the extra ½°, which leaves 55½°. So the complementary angle of 34½° is 55½°.

stepByStep.text: Two complementary angles add up to 90°. So we take 67½° away from 90°.
Take away the whole degrees first. 90° take away 67° leaves 23°.
Now take away the extra half of a degree. 23° take away ½° leaves 22½°.
The complementary angle of 67½° is 22½°.

misconceptions.A: This is close to what you get by taking the angle away from 180°. Complementary angles add up to 90°, so take 67½° away from 90°.
misconceptions.B: 90° is the right number to start from, but check the tens when you subtract. 90° − 67° is 23°, and there is still half a degree to take away.
misconceptions.C: Yes! 67½° and 22½° add up to exactly 90°, so they are complementary.
misconceptions.D: You took away the 67° well, since 90° − 67° = 23°. The extra ½° still has to be taken away, so the answer is a little less than 23°.

questionText: What is the supplementary angle of 55°?
hints: This question is about supplementary angles. Remember what two supplementary angles add up to, and then find the missing part.
Two supplementary angles add up to 180°, a straight line. So take 55° away from 180°.
A similar example: find the supplementary angle of 70°. Supplementary angles add up to 180°, and 180° − 70° = 110°. So the supplementary angle of 70° is 110°.

stepByStep.text: Two supplementary angles add up to 180°, like the two angles on a straight line.
Take 55° away from 180° to find the other angle.
The supplementary angle of 55° is 125°.

misconceptions.A: 180° is the right number to start from, but check the subtraction. 55° and 135° add up to 190°, which is too much.
misconceptions.B: 35° and 55° add up to 90°, so this is the complementary angle. Supplementary angles add up to 180°.
misconceptions.C: Yes! 55° and 125° add up to exactly 180°, so they are supplementary.
misconceptions.D: This takes 55° away from 360°, a full turn. Supplementary angles add up to 180°, a straight line.

questionText: What is the supplement of an angle of 10°?
hints: This is about supplementary angles. Two angles are supplementary when together they make a straight line.
Supplementary angles add up to 180°. So take 10° away from 180°.
Similar example: the supplement of 70° is 180° − 70° = 110°. Check: 70° + 110° = 180°.

stepByStep.text: Supplementary angles add up to 180°.
Take the given angle away from 180°.
Check by adding: 10° + 170° = 180°. The supplement of 10° is 170°.

misconceptions.A: Close, but this is 10° too small. Check the tens when you take 10° away from 180°.
misconceptions.B: Yes! 10° + 170° = 180°, so the supplement is 170°.
misconceptions.C: This is too big. The two angles together make only 180°, so the supplement must be smaller than 180°.
misconceptions.D: 180° is the total the two angles make together. Take 10° away from it.

questionText: If x + 35° = 90°, what is the supplement of x?
hints: This question has two parts. First find the angle x, and then find its supplement. Supplementary angles add up to 180°.
Start with x + 35° = 90°. Ask yourself what must be added to 35° to make 90°. That number is x, and you still need its supplement after that.
A similar example: if y + 20° = 90°, then y = 90° − 20° = 70°. The supplement of y is what you add to 70° to make 180°, and 180° − 70° = 110°. So the supplement of y is 110°.

stepByStep.text: First find x. It is the angle that adds to 35° to make 90°, so take 35° away from 90°. That gives x = 55°.
The question asks for the supplement of x, not x itself. Supplementary angles add up to 180°.
Take 55° away from 180°. The supplement of x is 125°.

misconceptions.A: 145° is the supplement of 35°. The question asks for the supplement of x, so find x first and then take it away from 180°.
misconceptions.B: Yes! x is 55°, and 55° and 125° add up to 180°.
misconceptions.C: 55° is x itself, so you have done the first part well. Now find the supplement of x by taking it away from 180°.
misconceptions.D: 90° is what x and 35° add up to. Find x first, and then find the angle that adds to x to make 180°.

questionText: The supplement of an angle is 125°. What is its complement?
hints: This question uses two ideas together. A supplement is measured against 180° and a complement is measured against 90°. You need to find the angle itself first.
The angle and its supplement add up to 180°. So take 125° away from 180° to find the angle. After that, find what must be added to the angle to make 90°.
A similar example: the supplement of an angle is 110°. The angle is 180° − 110° = 70°. Its complement is 90° − 70° = 20°. So the complement is 20°.

stepByStep.text: An angle and its supplement add up to 180°. So the angle is 180° take away 125°, which is 55°.
An angle and its complement add up to 90°. So take 55° away from 90°.
The complement of the angle is 35°.

misconceptions.A: An angle has no complement only when it is 90° or more. Here the angle is 180° − 125° = 55°, which is less than 90°, so it does have one.
misconceptions.B: Yes! The angle is 55°, and 55° and 35° add up to 90°.
misconceptions.C: 55° is the angle itself, so the first part is done well. Now find its complement by taking it away from 90°.
misconceptions.D: Check the first subtraction. 180° − 125° gives the angle, and then that angle is taken away from 90° to find its complement.

questionText: When two lines cross, how many pairs of vertically opposite angles are formed?
questionLatex: \text{Two intersecting lines form ? pairs of vertically opposite angles}
hints: This question is about the angles made when two straight lines cross, like the letter X. Vertically opposite angles are the ones that face each other across the crossing point.
Draw two lines crossing and number the angles 1, 2, 3 and 4 going round the point. Now match each angle with the one directly across from it, and count the matches.

A similar example: the same two crossing lines also make pairs of angles that sit side by side. Going round the point, these are angles 1 and 2, 2 and 3, 3 and 4, and 4 and 1, so there are 4 side by side pairs. Count the pairs that sit across from each other in the same careful way.

stepByStep.text: Two crossing lines make 4 angles around the point where they cross. Number them 1, 2, 3 and 4 going round.
Angle 1 is directly across from angle 3, so they make one pair. Angle 2 is directly across from angle 4, so they make another pair.
Every angle is now in a pair. So 2 pairs of vertically opposite angles are formed.

misconceptions.A: Try drawing the two lines and numbering the 4 angles. Each angle has just one partner directly across from it, so count those pairs again.
misconceptions.B: Yes! The 4 angles match up across the crossing point into 2 pairs.
misconceptions.C: 4 is the number of angles, not the number of pairs. Match each angle with the one directly across from it and count the pairs.
misconceptions.D: There is one more pair to find. The two crossing lines make 4 angles, and each one has a partner directly across from it.

questionText: Two lines intersect. One of the angles is 70°. What is the angle opposite to it?
hints: When two straight lines cross, they make four angles. The angles that face each other across the crossing point have a special link.
Picture the letter X. Look at the angle of 70° and the angle directly across from it, and remember what is true about vertically opposite angles.
Here is a similar one: two lines cross and one angle is 40°. Vertically opposite angles are equal, so the angle facing it is also 40°.

stepByStep.text: Two crossing lines make two pairs of angles that face each other. These are called vertically opposite angles.
Vertically opposite angles are always equal.
So the angle opposite to 70° is also 70°.

misconceptions.A: 20° comes from 90° − 70°. That works for two angles that make a right angle, but these two angles face each other across the crossing.
misconceptions.B: 290° comes from 360° − 70°, which is all the rest of the turn around the point. The question asks only for the one angle that faces 70°.
misconceptions.C: 110° comes from 180° − 70°. That is the angle next to 70° on the straight line, and the question asks for the one opposite it.
misconceptions.D: Yes! Vertically opposite angles are equal, so the angle facing 70° is also 70°.

questionText: What is the supplement of an angle of 85°?
hints: This is about supplementary angles. Two angles are supplementary when together they make a straight line.
Supplementary angles add up to 180°. So take 85° away from 180°.
Similar example: the supplement of 70° is 180° − 70° = 110°. Check: 70° + 110° = 180°.

stepByStep.text: Supplementary angles add up to 180°.
Take the given angle away from 180°.
Check by adding: 85° + 95° = 180°. The supplement of 85° is 95°.

misconceptions.A: Close, but this is 10° too big. Check the tens when you take 85° away from 180°.
misconceptions.B: This is too big. The two angles together make only 180°, so the supplement must be smaller than 180°.
misconceptions.C: Yes! 85° + 95° = 180°, so the supplement is 95°.
misconceptions.D: This is the angle itself. The supplement is what you add to 85° to make 180°.

questionText: Two adjacent angles form a linear pair. If one angle is 65°, what is the other?
hints: This question is about a linear pair. The two angles sit side by side on a straight line, so think about what they add up to together.
A straight line makes an angle of 180°. The two angles share it, so take 65° away from 180°.
A similar example: two angles form a linear pair and one of them is 110°. Together they make 180°, so the other is 180° − 110° = 70°.

stepByStep.text: The two angles of a linear pair sit on a straight line, so they add up to 180°.
Take 65° away from 180° to find the other angle.
The other angle is 115°.

misconceptions.A: 25° and 65° add up to 90°, a right angle. A linear pair sits on a straight line, so the two angles add up to 180°.
misconceptions.B: The two angles of a linear pair are not always equal. They add up to 180°, so take 65° away from 180°.
misconceptions.C: Yes! 65° and 115° add up to 180°, a straight line.
misconceptions.D: This takes 65° away from 360°, a full turn. A linear pair makes a straight line, which is 180°.

questionText: What is the angle between the hour hand and the minute hand at 3 o'clock?
hints: This question is about the angle between the hands of a clock. The 12 numbers split the clock face into 12 equal gaps, so first think about how big one gap is.
A full turn is 360° and the clock has 12 equal gaps, so each gap is 360° ÷ 12 = 30°. At 3 o'clock the minute hand points at 12 and the hour hand points at 3. Count the gaps between them.
A similar example: at 5 o'clock the minute hand points at 12 and the hour hand points at 5. That is 5 gaps, and each gap is 30°, so the angle is 5 × 30° = 150°.

stepByStep.text: The clock face is a full turn of 360°, split into 12 equal gaps. Each gap is 30°.
At 3 o'clock the minute hand points at 12 and the hour hand points at 3. There are 3 gaps between them.
Three gaps of 30° make 90°. The angle between the hands at 3 o'clock is 90°.

misconceptions.A: 30° is the size of just one gap between two numbers on the clock. From 12 to 3 there are 3 gaps.
misconceptions.B: Yes! From 12 to 3 is 3 gaps of 30°, which makes a right angle.
misconceptions.C: 120° is 4 gaps, which is the angle at 4 o'clock. Count the gaps from 12 to 3 again.
misconceptions.D: 60° is 2 gaps, which is the angle at 2 o'clock. Count the gaps from 12 to 3 again.

questionText: Find the angle between the hour hand and the minute hand at 9:30.
hints: This is a clock angle question with a catch. At half past the hour, the hour hand is no longer pointing exactly at a number, so think about where each hand really is.
At 9:30 the minute hand points at 6. The hour hand has moved halfway from 9 to 10. Count the gaps from 6 up to that halfway point, remembering that each full gap is 30°.
A similar example: at 7:30 the minute hand points at 6 and the hour hand is halfway between 7 and 8. From 6 to 7 is 1 full gap, which is 30°. Half a gap more is 15°. So the angle is 30° + 15° = 45°.

stepByStep.text: At 9:30 the minute hand points at 6. The hour hand does not point at 9. In half an hour it has moved halfway from 9 to 10.
Each gap between two numbers is 30°. From 6 to 9 is 3 gaps, which is 90°.
The hour hand is half a gap past 9. Half of 30° is 15°.
Add the two parts together. The angle between the hands at 9:30 is 105°.

misconceptions.A: 90° would be right if the hour hand were still pointing exactly at 9. By 9:30 it has moved halfway towards 10, so the angle is a little bigger.
misconceptions.B: Yes! From 6 to 9 is 90°, and the hour hand is another 15° past the 9.
misconceptions.C: 120° would be right if the hour hand had already reached 10. At 9:30 it is only halfway between 9 and 10.
misconceptions.D: The angle is in the list. Put the minute hand on 6 and the hour hand halfway between 9 and 10, then count the gaps at 30° each.

questionText: What is the supplement of an angle of 165°?
hints: This is about supplementary angles. Two angles are supplementary when together they make a straight line.
Supplementary angles add up to 180°. So take 165° away from 180°.
Similar example: the supplement of 70° is 180° − 70° = 110°. Check: 70° + 110° = 180°.

stepByStep.text: Supplementary angles add up to 180°.
Take the given angle away from 180°.
Check by adding: 165° + 15° = 180°. The supplement of 165° is 15°.

misconceptions.A: Close, but this is 10° too small. Check the tens when you take 165° away from 180°.
misconceptions.B: This is too big. The two angles together make only 180°, so the supplement must be smaller than 180°.
misconceptions.C: Close, but this is 10° too big. Check the tens when you take 165° away from 180°.
misconceptions.D: Yes! 165° + 15° = 180°, so the supplement is 15°.

questionText: At which of these times will the angle between the clock hands be obtuse?
hints: This question joins two ideas, clock angles and the names of angles. An obtuse angle is more than 90° but less than 180°, so you need the angle at each time.
Each gap between two numbers on the clock is 30°. Start with the o'clock times, where the hour hand points exactly at a number, and count the gaps between the two hands.

A similar example: at 5:00 the minute hand points at 12 and the hour hand points at 5. That is 5 gaps, and 5 × 30° = 150°. Since 150° is between 90° and 180°, the angle at 5:00 is obtuse. Test each time in the list in the same way.

stepByStep.text: Each gap between two numbers on a clock is 30°. An obtuse angle is more than 90° and less than 180°.
At 10:00 the hands are 2 gaps apart, which is 60°. That is less than 90°, so it is acute.
At 6:00 the hands are 6 gaps apart, which is 180°. That is a straight angle, not an obtuse one.
At 3:30 the minute hand is on 6 and the hour hand is halfway between 3 and 4. That is 2 and a half gaps, which is 75°, so it is acute.
At 4:00 the hands are 4 gaps apart, which is 120°. That is between 90° and 180°, so the angle is obtuse at 4:00.

misconceptions.A: At 3:30 the hour hand has moved halfway from 3 to 4, so the hands are only 2 and a half gaps apart. That is 75°, which is less than 90°.
misconceptions.B: Yes! At 4:00 the hands are 4 gaps apart, and 4 × 30° = 120°, which is between 90° and 180°.
misconceptions.C: At 10:00 the hands are only 2 gaps apart, which is 60°. That is an acute angle, so look for a time with a wider gap.
misconceptions.D: At 6:00 the hands point in opposite directions and make exactly 180°. That is a straight angle, and an obtuse angle must be less than 180°.

questionText: When will the hour hand and the minute hand form a straight angle (180°)?
hints: This is a clock angle question. A straight angle means the two hands point in exactly opposite directions, so think carefully about where the hour hand really is at each time.
The hour hand points exactly at a number only at an o'clock time. At 3:45 and at 9:15 it has already moved away from its number. Check whether the hands are still exactly opposite at those times.

A similar example: at 3:00 the minute hand is on 12 and the hour hand is exactly on 3, so the angle is 3 × 30° = 90°. At 12:15 the minute hand is on 3, but the hour hand has crept a little past 12, so the angle is a little less than 90°.

stepByStep.text: At 6:00 the minute hand is on 12 and the hour hand is exactly on 6. They are 6 gaps apart, and each gap is 30°, so the angle is 180°.
At 3:45 the minute hand is on 9, but the hour hand has moved most of the way from 3 to 4. The hands are not exactly opposite.
At 9:15 the minute hand is on 3, but the hour hand has moved a little past 9. The hands are not exactly opposite here either.
So the hands form a straight angle only at 6:00.

misconceptions.A: At 3:45 the minute hand is on 9, but the hour hand is no longer on 3. It has moved most of the way to 4, so the hands are not exactly opposite.
misconceptions.B: Yes! At 6:00 one hand points straight up and the other straight down, which makes 180°.
misconceptions.C: At 9:15 the minute hand is on 3, but the hour hand has moved a little past 9. That makes the angle a bit less than 180°.
misconceptions.D: It looks that way if the hour hand stays on its number. At 3:45 and 9:15 the hour hand has moved on, so only one of these times gives exactly 180°.

questionText: At which of these times is the angle between the clock hands the GREATEST?
hints: Work out the angle between the hands for each time, then compare. Remember that the hour hand keeps moving slowly as the minutes pass.
The clock face has 12 gaps of 30° each. For each time, find where the minute hand points, find where the hour hand is, and count the gaps between them. Start with 9:00.
Similar example: at 3:30 the minute hand is on the 6. The hour hand is halfway between 3 and 4. From there to the 6 is 2 and a half gaps, and 2.5 × 30° = 75°.

stepByStep.text: The clock has 12 gaps between the numbers, and each gap is 30°.
At 9:00 the hands are on 9 and 12, which is 3 gaps.
At 4:30 the minute hand is on 6 and the hour hand is halfway between 4 and 5. That is 1 and a half gaps.
At 12:15 the minute hand is on 3. The hour hand has moved a quarter of a gap past 12, so there are 2 and three-quarter gaps between them.
At 6:15 the minute hand is on 3. The hour hand is a quarter of a gap past 6, so there are 3 and a quarter gaps between them.
Compare 45°, 97.5°, 90° and 82.5°. The greatest angle is 97.5°, at 6:15.

misconceptions.A: At 4:30 the hour hand is halfway between 4 and 5, only 1 and a half gaps from the minute hand. That is 45°, the smallest of the four.
misconceptions.B: Yes! At 6:15 the hands are 3 and a quarter gaps apart, which is 97.5°. That is more than 90°, 82.5° and 45°.
misconceptions.C: At 9:00 the angle is exactly 90°. One of the other times gives a little more than 90°, so check where the hour hand is at 6:15.
misconceptions.D: At 12:15 the hour hand has moved a little past 12 towards the minute hand, so the angle is 82.5°, a little less than 90°.

questionText: At 1 o'clock, the angle between clock hands is 30°. At what time will the angle be complementary to this?
hints: Two angles are complementary when they add up to a right angle. First find the angle you need, then find a time when the clock hands make it.
Work out what must be added to 30° to make 90°. That is the angle the clock hands have to make.

Here is a similar one: at which o'clock time do the hands make an angle supplementary to 60°? Supplementary angles add up to 180°, so the angle needed is 180° − 60° = 120°. Each gap between numbers is 30°, and 120 ÷ 30 = 4 gaps, so the time is 4 o'clock.

stepByStep.text: Complementary angles add up to 90°. So the angle we need is 90° − 30° = 60°.
At 1 o'clock the hands are one number apart and the angle is 30°. So each gap between numbers on the clock is 30°.
60° is two gaps, because 60 ÷ 30 = 2.
The hands are two gaps apart at 2 o'clock. So the time is 2 o'clock.

misconceptions.A: At 7 o'clock the hands are 5 gaps apart the short way round, which is 5 × 30° = 150°. Complementary angles add up to 90°, so look for a much smaller angle.
misconceptions.B: At 6 o'clock the hands make a straight line, which is 180°. The angle you need adds to 30° to make 90°.
misconceptions.C: At 5 o'clock the angle is 150°, and 30° + 150° = 180°. That pair is supplementary, and complementary angles add up to 90°.
misconceptions.D: Yes! The complement of 30° is 60°, which is two gaps of 30°, and the hands are two gaps apart at 2 o'clock.

questionText: What is the complement of an angle of 27°?
hints: This is about complementary angles. Two angles are complementary when together they make a right angle.
Complementary angles add up to 90°. So take 27° away from 90°.
Similar example: the complement of 20° is 90° − 20° = 70°. Check: 20° + 70° = 90°.

stepByStep.text: Complementary angles add up to 90°.
Take the given angle away from 90°.
Check by adding: 27° + 63° = 90°. The complement of 27° is 63°.

misconceptions.A: Close, but this is 10° too big. Check the tens when you take 27° away from 90°.
misconceptions.B: Yes! 27° + 63° = 90°, so the complement is 63°.
misconceptions.C: Close, but this is 10° too small. Check the tens when you take 27° away from 90°.
misconceptions.D: This is too big. The two angles together make only 90°, so the complement must be smaller than 90°.

questionText: What is the complement of an angle of 85°?
hints: This is about complementary angles. Two angles are complementary when together they make a right angle.
Complementary angles add up to 90°. Think about how much more 85° needs to reach 90°.
Similar example: the complement of 40° is 90° − 40° = 50°. Check: 40° + 50° = 90°.

stepByStep.text: Complementary angles add up to 90°, which is a right angle.
Take the given angle away from 90°: 90 − 85 = 5.
Check by adding: 85° + 5° = 90°. The complement of 85° is 5°.

misconceptions.A: 15° is 100 − 85. Complementary angles add up to 90°, not 100°.
misconceptions.B: 95° is 180 − 85, which fits a straight line. Complementary angles make a right angle together.
misconceptions.C: 355° is far bigger than a right angle. The angle and its complement together make only 90°.
misconceptions.D: That's it! 85 + 5 = 90, a right angle, so the complement is 5°.

questionText: What is the angle between North-East and South directions?
hints: This question is about directions on a compass. The four main directions are a quarter turn apart, and the in-between directions sit exactly halfway.
North, East, South and West are 90° apart. North-East is halfway between North and East. Go from North-East to East first, and then on from East to South.
A similar example: find the angle between North-East and North-West. From North-East to North is half of 90°, which is 45°. From North to North-West is another 45°. So the angle is 45° + 45° = 90°.

stepByStep.text: North, East, South and West are each 90° apart. North-East is exactly halfway between North and East.
From North-East to East is half of 90°, which is 45°.
From East to South is one quarter turn, which is 90°.
Add the two parts. The angle between North-East and South is 135°.

misconceptions.A: 90° is the turn from East to South. North-East is 45° before East, so that part has to be added too.
misconceptions.B: Check the two parts of the turn. North-East to East is 45° and East to South is 90°, so add those together.
misconceptions.C: Yes! North-East to East is 45° and East to South is 90°, which makes 135° altogether.
misconceptions.D: 45° only takes you from North-East to East. You still need to turn from East to South.

questionText: How many degrees does the hour hand move in one hour?
hints: This question is about how fast the hour hand turns. Think about how long the hour hand takes to go once all the way round the clock.
The hour hand makes one full turn of 360° in 12 hours. Share 360° equally among the 12 hours.
A similar example: how far does the hour hand turn in 3 hours? It turns 360° in 12 hours, and 3 hours is one quarter of 12 hours. One quarter of 360° is 360° ÷ 4 = 90°. So it turns 90° in 3 hours.

stepByStep.text: The hour hand goes once round the clock in 12 hours. One full turn is 360°.
Share 360° equally among the 12 hours.
The hour hand moves 30° in one hour.

misconceptions.A: 360° is a full turn, and the hour hand needs 12 hours for that. Share 360° among the 12 hours to find the turn in one hour.
misconceptions.B: 6° is how far the minute hand moves in one minute. The hour hand takes 12 hours for a full turn, so divide 360° by 12.
misconceptions.C: Yes! In one hour the hour hand moves from one number to the next, which is 360° ÷ 12.
misconceptions.D: 60 is the number of minutes in an hour, not the number of degrees. Share the full turn of 360° among 12 hours.

questionText: What is the complement of an angle of 8°?
hints: This is about complementary angles. Two angles are complementary when together they make a right angle.
Complementary angles add up to 90°. Think about how much more 8° needs to reach 90°.
Similar example: the complement of 35° is 90° − 35° = 55°. Check: 35° + 55° = 90°.

stepByStep.text: Complementary angles add up to 90°, which is a right angle.
Take the given angle away from 90°: 90 − 8 = 82.
Check by adding: 8° + 82° = 90°. The complement of 8° is 82°.

misconceptions.A: Yes! Complementary angles add up to 90°, and 90 − 8 = 82.
misconceptions.B: 72° is close, but 8 + 72 makes only 80. Look at the tens again in your subtraction.
misconceptions.C: 278° is much too big. A complement is always smaller than 90°, because the two angles share one right angle.
misconceptions.D: 92° is 100 − 8. The two angles make a right angle together, and a right angle is not 100°.

questionText: How many degrees does the minute hand move in 1 minute?
hints: This question is about how fast the minute hand turns. Think about how long the minute hand takes to go once all the way round the clock.
The minute hand makes one full turn of 360° in 60 minutes. Share 360° equally among the 60 minutes.

A similar example: how far does the minute hand turn in 15 minutes? It turns 360° in 60 minutes, and 15 minutes is one quarter of that time. One quarter of 360° is 360° ÷ 4 = 90°. So it turns 90° in 15 minutes.

stepByStep.text: The minute hand goes once round the clock in 60 minutes. One full turn is 360°.
Share 360° equally among the 60 minutes.
The minute hand moves 6° in 1 minute.

misconceptions.A: Check the sharing. The full turn of 360° is shared among 60 minutes, so work out 360° ÷ 60.
misconceptions.B: 1° each minute would make only 60° in an hour. The minute hand turns a full 360° in 60 minutes, so each minute is more than 1°.
misconceptions.C: 30° is how far the minute hand moves in 5 minutes, from one number to the next. One minute is a much smaller turn.
misconceptions.D: Yes! 360° shared among 60 minutes is 6° for each minute.

questionText: Two complementary angles are in the ratio 2:3. Find the smaller angle.
hints: This question joins complementary angles with a ratio. First decide what the two angles add up to, and then share that total in the ratio.
Complementary angles add up to 90°. The ratio 2:3 means 2 equal parts and 3 equal parts, so there are 5 equal parts altogether. Find the size of one part first.
A similar example: two complementary angles are in the ratio 4:5. There are 4 + 5 = 9 parts, so one part is 90° ÷ 9 = 10°. The smaller angle is 4 × 10° = 40° and the larger is 5 × 10° = 50°.

stepByStep.text: Complementary angles add up to 90°. The ratio 2:3 means there are 5 equal parts altogether.
Find one part by sharing 90° into 5 equal parts.
The smaller angle has 2 of these parts.
The larger angle is 3 × 18° = 54°, and 36° + 54° = 90°. So the smaller angle is 36°.

misconceptions.A: Yes! One part is 18°, and the smaller angle has 2 parts, which is 36°.
misconceptions.B: 54° is the larger angle, with 3 parts. The question asks for the smaller angle, which has 2 parts.
misconceptions.C: This shares 180° in the ratio. Complementary angles add up to 90°, so share 90° into 5 parts.
misconceptions.D: Check the size of one part. There are 2 + 3 = 5 parts in 90°, so one part is 90° ÷ 5, and the smaller angle is 2 of them.

questionText: What is the supplement of an angle of 118°?
hints: This is about supplementary angles. Two angles are supplementary when together they make a straight line.
Supplementary angles add up to 180°. So take 118° away from 180°.
Similar example: the supplement of 70° is 180° − 70° = 110°. Check: 70° + 110° = 180°.

stepByStep.text: Supplementary angles add up to 180°.
Take the given angle away from 180°.
Check by adding: 118° + 62° = 180°. The supplement of 118° is 62°.

misconceptions.A: Yes! 118° + 62° = 180°, so the supplement is 62°.
misconceptions.B: Close, but this is 10° too big. Check the tens when you take 118° away from 180°.
misconceptions.C: Close, but this is 10° too small. Check the tens when you take 118° away from 180°.
misconceptions.D: This is too big. The two angles together make only 180°, so the supplement must be smaller than 180°.

questionText: Two supplementary angles differ by 40°. Find the larger angle.
hints: This is a sum and difference question. You know what the two angles add up to and how far apart they are, and you need the bigger one.
Supplementary angles add up to 180°. Take the extra 40° away from 180° first. What is left is two equal shares, one for each angle.

A similar example: two supplementary angles differ by 30°. Take away the extra, 180° − 30° = 150°. Halve it to get the smaller angle, 150° ÷ 2 = 75°. The larger is 75° + 30° = 105°. Check: 105° + 75° = 180°.

stepByStep.text: Supplementary angles add up to 180°. The larger angle is the smaller angle with 40° extra.
Take the extra 40° away from the total. What is left is two copies of the smaller angle.
Halve 140° to find the smaller angle.
Add the extra 40° back to get the larger angle. Check that 110° + 70° = 180°. The larger angle is 110°.

misconceptions.A: If the larger angle were 100°, the other would be 80°. They add up to 180°, but they differ by only 20°, and the question says 40°.
misconceptions.B: Yes! 110° and 70° add up to 180° and differ by exactly 40°.
misconceptions.C: If the larger angle were 120°, the other would be 60°. They differ by 60°, and the question says 40°.
misconceptions.D: 80° is less than half of 180°, so it cannot be the larger of the two angles. Take 40° away from 180°, halve what is left, and then add the 40° back.

questionText: Three angles meeting at a point are 110°, 85°, and x°. Find x.
questionLatex: 110° + 85° + x° + ? = 360°. \text{ If only 3 angles, find } x.
hints: This question is about angles that meet at a point. Together they go all the way round the point, so think about what a full turn measures.
Angles around a point add up to 360°. Add the two angles you know, 110° and 85°, and then take that total away from 360°.
A similar example: three angles meeting at a point are 120°, 100° and y°. The two known angles add up to 120° + 100° = 220°. So y = 360° − 220° = 140°.

stepByStep.text: The three angles go all the way round the point, so they add up to 360°.
Add the two angles you know.
Take this away from the full turn to find the third angle.
So x is 165°.

misconceptions.A: With 75°, the three angles add up to only 110° + 85° + 75° = 270°. Angles around a point make a full turn of 360°.
misconceptions.B: 155° comes from adding 110° + 85° as 205° and then working out 360° − 205°. Add 110° and 85° once more, tens first.
misconceptions.C: 175° comes from adding 110° + 85° as 185°, leaving out the carried ten, and then 360° − 185°. Check the adding again.
misconceptions.D: Yes! 110° + 85° = 195°, and 360° − 195° = 165°, so the three angles make a full turn.

questionText: What is the complement of an angle of 55°?
hints: This is about complementary angles. Two angles are complementary when together they make a right angle.
Complementary angles add up to 90°. So take 55° away from 90°.
Similar example: the complement of 20° is 90° − 20° = 70°. Check: 20° + 70° = 90°.

stepByStep.text: Complementary angles add up to 90°.
Take the given angle away from 90°.
Check by adding: 55° + 35° = 90°. The complement of 55° is 35°.

misconceptions.A: Yes! 55° + 35° = 90°, so the complement is 35°.
misconceptions.B: Close, but this is 10° too big. Check the tens when you take 55° away from 90°.
misconceptions.C: Close, but this is 10° too small. Check the tens when you take 55° away from 90°.
misconceptions.D: This is too big. The two angles together make only 90°, so the complement must be smaller than 90°.

questionText: Angles on a straight line are x°, 2x°, and 3x°. Find x.
hints: This question is about angles on a straight line. Think about what they add up to, and how many equal shares of x there are altogether.
Angles on a straight line add up to 180°. The angles are 1 lot of x, 2 lots of x and 3 lots of x. Count how many lots of x that is altogether.
A similar example: the angles on a straight line are y° and 4y°. That is 1 + 4 = 5 lots of y, and they add up to 180°. So y = 180° ÷ 5 = 36°. Check: 36° + 144° = 180°.

stepByStep.text: Angles on a straight line add up to 180°.
The angles are 1 lot of x, 2 lots of x and 3 lots of x. That is 6 lots of x altogether.
